title: Week 1: Introduction to Data Science

Why R?

Designed specifically for statistics and data analysis
Ecosystem of packages for data manipulation, visualization, and modeling
Support for reproducible research (RMarkdown, Quarto)
Strong community and extensive documentation
Seamless integration with other tools and languages
Free and open source

title: Reproducible Research and Project Management
text:
Scenario

We have been given some legacy R code and asked to “tidy it up” and produce a report based on it.
We’ll do so with Quarto + Git.

title: Reproducible Research and Project Management
text:
What is Git?

Git is a source control system.
Provides mechanisms for:

Backing up.
Checkpointing code.
Developing new features without breaking working code.
Collaboration.

title: Reproducible Research and Project Management
text:

git init
git add
git commit
Connecting with GitHub
git push

title: Reproducible Research and Project Management
text:
What is “Literate Programming”?
Literate programming is a methodology introduced by Donald Knuth, whereby:

Explanations are written alongside code
The document can be “rendered” (“knitted”) to produce a readable report.
Changes in code are automatically reflected in the output to reduce manual mistakes.

Frameworks like Quarto implement Literate programming.

title: Reproducible Research and Project Management
text:
Solution: Branches



Git Branch Workflow, from Wikipedia

title: Reproducible Research and Project Management
text:
Branching

Check branch with git branch
Create a branch with git branch my-amazing-feature
Switch to the branch with git checkout my-amazing-feature.
Work as normal on the branch, without affecting main.

title: Reproducible Research and Project Management
text:
Merging
We often need to merge changes between branches. This is done using git merge.
Once done making changes on my-amazing-feature:

Return to main with git checkout main
Merge changes with git merge my-amazing-feature
Enter a message
Push to GitHub.

title: Reproducible Research and Project Management
text:
Merge Conflicts
When you run git merge git will “pick up” commits from my-amazing-feature and put them on `main.

title: Coding in R
text:
Objectives
By the end of this lecture you will be able to:


create and inspect R’s core data structures — variables, vectors, lists and data frames




make vectorised decisions with if_else() and case_when(), instead of loops




write functions and compose them with the pipe, |>

title: Coding in R
text:
Packages

install.packages("dplyr")   # ONCE, in the console
library(dplyr)              # EVERY new session







Never put install.packages() in a .qmd


Quarto re-runs every chunk on every render — the package would be re-installed from CRAN each time you render.
Rule: Install in the console; load with library() in the document.

title: Coding in R
text:
Your first variables






Task


Create three variables — a number, some text, and a truth value — then ask R what type each one is.





x <- 5
y <- "Hello"
z <- TRUE

typeof(x)

[1] "double"

typeof(y)

[1] "character"

typeof(z)

[1] "logical"




Point out double, character, logical. Mention the chapter’s aside: <- is idiomatic R, = is fine, both accepted in assessments.

title: Coding in R
text:
R is dynamically typed






Task


Demonstrate dynamic typing in R





number <- 5
typeof(number)

[1] "double"

number <- "hello"
typeof(number)

[1] "character"




R does not require variable types. It also does not check types when you call a function!

title: Coding in R
text:
Building vectors






Task


Make a vector of the numbers 1 to 5 with c(), then check its type and length. What happens if you check the length of the plain number x from before?





vector <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

typeof(vector)   # still "double"!

[1] "double"

length(vector)

[1] 5

length(x)        # scalars ARE length-1 vectors

[1] 1




In R there are no scalars — everything is a vector.

title: Coding in R
text:
Indexing: R counts from 1






Task


Get the 2nd element, the 5th element, and elements 2 through 4.





vector[2]

[1] 2

vector[5]     # the LAST element — it would be index 4 in Python!

[1] 5

vector[2:4]

[1] 2 3 4




Show vector[0]: it returns an empty vector, no error.

title: Coding in R
text:
Logical indexing






Task


Use a vector of TRUE/FALSE to pick out elements — then negate it with ! to pick the others.





elements <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)

vector[elements]    # positions 1, 3, 4

[1] 1 3 4

vector[!elements]   # elementwise negation: positions 2, 5

[1] 2 5




This is the idiom that powers filtering data in every week to come.

title: Coding in R
text:
Lists: containers for anything






Task


Build a list about a penguin — two bits of text, a numeric vector, and a count — then pull out elements by name and by position.





l <- list(
  name = "Flipper",
  species = "Adelie",
  measurements = c(210, 217, 230),
  n_measurements = 3
)

l$name

[1] "Flipper"

l$measurements

[1] 210 217 230

l[[3]]

[1] 210 217 230




Demo the difference between [3] and [[3]] - a list vs. the element. Comment on why the names might be better than the numbers.

title: Coding in R
section: Data frames: lists of equal-length vectors
text:
Data frames: lists of equal-length vectors






Task


Build a small table of penguins — name, species, flipper length — then get a column with $, a row with [2, ], and a single entry.





df <- data.frame(
  name              = c("Flipper", "Tux", "Pingu"),
  species           = c("Adelie", "Gentoo", "Emperor"),
  flipper_length_mm = c(210, 217, 230)
)

df

     name species flipper_length_mm
1 Flipper  Adelie               210
2     Tux  Gentoo               217
3   Pingu Emperor               230

df$name              # access a column

[1] "Flipper" "Tux"     "Pingu"  

df$flipper_length_mm

[1] 210 217 230

df[2, ]              # row 2

  name species flipper_length_mm
2  Tux  Gentoo               217

df[2, "species"]     # single entry

[1] "Gentoo"









Tibbles


Data frames have a modern cousin, the tibble (tidyverse). Same functionality, nicer printing. We’ll switch to tibble in the data weeks — for today data.frame is fine.

title: Coding in R
Coding in R
text:
if_else: a vectorised conditional






Task


Classify each element of x <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5) as “big” or “small” depending on whether it exceeds 2.





library(dplyr)
x <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5)

if_else(x > 2, "big", "small")

[1] "big"   "small" "big"   "small" "big"

title: Coding in R
text:
case_when: many conditions






Task


Classify x as “small” (< 2), “medium” (< 5), or “large” (everything else).





case_when(
  x < 2 ~ "small",
  x < 5 ~ "medium",
  TRUE  ~ "large"
)

[1] "medium" "small"  "medium" "small"  "large" 




Order matters: swap the first two conditions and “small” disappears.

title: Coding in R
text:
Writing Functions






Task


Write a function add(x, y).





add <- function(x, y) {
  x + y        # the LAST expression is the return value
}

add(1, 10)

[1] 11




No return() needed.

title: Coding in R
text:
Guard clauses: return






Task


Write clip(x, lower, upper) that forces a value into a range — e.g. for cleaning impossible measurements.





clip <- function(x, lower, upper) {
  if (x < lower) return(lower)   # guard clause
  if (x > upper) return(upper)
  x                              # still here? it's in range
}

clip(5, 0, 10)

[1] 5

clip(-3, 0, 10)

[1] 0

clip(42, 0, 10)

[1] 10




Note that you could also use case_when to do this

title: Coding in R
text:
Functions are Variables


sapply(1:10, function(x) clip(x, 3, 7))

 [1] 3 3 3 4 5 6 7 7 7 7




A function you never named — an anonymous function — passed straight into sapply.
It is called a “higher order function.”

title: Coding in R
text:
Composing functions: f(g(x))

times_ten <- function(y) y * 10
add_five <- function(x) x + 5

x <- 10
times_ten(add_five(x))


Readable — up to a point.

title: Coding in R
text:
The pipe: |>






Task


Implement the above logic using the pipe operator |>





x |> add_five() |> times_ten()

[1] 150




Much more readable.


The parentheses after each function are required — the pipe inserts the left-hand side into the FIRST argument.
Mention %>% (magrittr) exists and behaves almost identically, but |> is base R.

title: Coding in R
text:
When you’re stuck

?mean — documentation (also ?dplyr, even ?`+`)
example(mean) — run the docs’ examples
??"linear regression" — search all installed packages
Read the error message first — then search it verbatim online







AI tools


Great for getting unblocked — but they hallucinate. Verify everything with ?, and never paste sensitive data into them. The docs are always right; the AI is usually helpful.

title: Coding in R
text:
Guard clauses: return






ImportantTask



Write clip(x, lower, upper) that forces a value into a range — e.g. for cleaning impossible measurements.




clip <- function(x, lower, upper) {
  if (x < lower) return(lower)   # guard clause
  if (x > upper) return(upper)
  x                              # still here? it's in range
}

clip(5, 0, 10)

[1] 5

clip(-3, 0, 10)

[1] 0

clip(42, 0, 10)

[1] 10




Note that you could also use case_when to do this

title: Coding in R
text:
Functions are Variables


sapply(1:10, function(x) clip(x, 3, 7))

 [1] 3 3 3 4 5 6 7 7 7 7




A function you never named — an anonymous function — passed straight into sapply.
It is called a “higher order function.”

title: Coding in R
text:
Composing functions: f(g(x))

times_ten <- function(y) y * 10
add_five <- function(x) x + 5

x <- 10
times_ten(add_five(x))


Readable — up to a point.

title: Coding in R
text:
The pipe: |>






ImportantTask



Implement the above logic using the pipe operator |>




x |> add_five() |> times_ten()

[1] 150




Much more readable.


The parentheses after each function are required — the pipe inserts the left-hand side into the FIRST argument.
Mention %>% (magrittr) exists and behaves almost identically, but |> is base R.

title: Coding in R
text:
When you’re stuck

?mean — documentation (also ?dplyr, even ?`+`)
example(mean) — run the docs’ examples
??"linear regression" — search all installed packages
Read the error message first — then search it verbatim online







TipAI tools



Great for getting unblocked — but they hallucinate. Verify everything with ?, and never paste sensitive data into them. The docs are always right; the AI is usually helpful.
